tensor.simple: A block of numbers with axes, like a numpy array. Deep learning libraries call it a tensor.
tensor.example: A batch of 32 windows, 96 steps, 3 features has shape [32, 96, 3].

batch.simple: A group of examples that the model processes together in one step.
batch.example: A batch of 32 windows is a tensor with 32 rows on the first axis.

sliding window.simple: A frame of fixed length that moves along a series one step at a time. Each position gives one training example.
sliding window.example: Series 0 1 2 3 4 5 with frame length 5 gives two windows.

lookback window.simple: The past values that the model reads as input before it forecasts.
lookback window.example: A lookback of 96 hours means the model sees the last 4 days.

forecast horizon.simple: How many steps into the future you want to forecast.
forecast horizon.example: A horizon of 24 on hourly data is one day ahead.

leakage.simple: When information from the future, or from the test data, gets into training. The score then looks better than it really is.
leakage.example: Scaling with the mean of the whole series before the split leaks future information.

recurrent neural network.simple: A network that reads a sequence one step at a time and keeps a memory (hidden state) between steps.
recurrent neural network.example: An RNN reads 96 hours one by one, then predicts the next 24.

hidden state.simple: The memory vector of a recurrent network. It is updated at every time step.

vanishing gradient.simple: The training signal becomes almost zero when it travels back through many steps, so the network cannot learn long-range effects.
vanishing gradient.example: A signal multiplied by 0.9 at each step is below 1% after 44 steps.

LSTM.simple: A recurrent network with gates and a cell state. It can keep information over many steps.

GRU.simple: A lighter recurrent network with two gates and one memory. It has fewer parameters than an LSTM.
GRU.example: A GRU is often faster to train than an LSTM of the same size.

cell state.simple: The long-term memory line inside an LSTM. It is changed by adding, which keeps old information alive.

gate.simple: A number between 0 and 1 that works like a tap: 0 blocks a signal, 1 lets it pass.
gate.example: A forget gate of 0 erases that memory slot.

convolution.simple: A small list of weights (kernel) that slides along the series and computes a weighted sum at each position.
convolution.example: Kernel [1, 1] adds the current and the previous value.

causal convolution.simple: A convolution that uses only the current and past values, never the future. Padding is added on the left only.

receptive field.simple: How many past steps can change one output value of a convolution stack.
receptive field.example: Kernel 2 with dilations 1, 2, 4, 8 has a receptive field of 16.

residual connection.simple: A shortcut that adds the input of a block to its output. It helps deep networks train.

sequence-to-sequence.simple: A model with an encoder that reads the past and a decoder that writes the future, step by step.
sequence-to-sequence.example: The encoder reads 96 hours; the decoder writes the next 24.

teacher forcing.simple: In training, the decoder gets the real previous value instead of its own guess.
teacher forcing.example: At test time there are no real values, so the model must use its own forecasts.

likelihood.simple: How probable the real data are under the distribution that the model predicted.
likelihood.example: A model that predicts a normal curve centered near the real value has a high likelihood.

negative log-likelihood.simple: The loss −log(likelihood). Lower is better. It trains a model to predict a good distribution.

backcast.simple: In N-BEATS, a block's reconstruction of its input window. It is subtracted to leave a residual for the next block.
backcast.example: Input minus backcast is the residual.

basis function.simple: A ready-made shape, such as a line or a sine wave. A model can build a curve by scaling and adding basis functions.
basis function.example: Trend uses 1, t, t². Season uses sine and cosine.

gated residual network.simple: A small block of the Temporal Fusion Transformer that can switch itself down with a gate when its work is not needed.
gated residual network.example: It helps TFT ignore useless inputs.

variable selection.simple: A step that learns a weight for each input feature, so useless features get low weight.
variable selection.example: Weights 0.7, 0.25, 0.05 show that the first feature matters most.

attention.simple: A layer where each position looks at all other positions and takes a weighted average of them.
attention.example: A forecast for Monday can look at the last Monday.

self-attention.simple: Attention where the sequence looks at itself. Each token makes a query, a key and a value.

distribution shift.simple: The data in use have a different mean, spread or pattern than the training data.
distribution shift.example: Sales level moves from 100 to 300 after a new product launch.

state-space model.simple: A model with a hidden state that is updated by a linear rule at each step. It can run as a loop or as a long convolution.

global model.simple: One model trained on many series together.
global model.example: A LightGBM model with lag features for all products.

quantile.simple: A cut point of a distribution. The 0.9 quantile has 90% of the outcomes below it.
quantile.example: P50 is the median; P90 is the 0.9 quantile.
